flagged.issue: 몰다 means to drive (a car, a herd of animals), not to ride a bicycle. The standard Korean collocation for bicycles is 자전거를 타다. 자전거를 몰다 is unnatural and would strike native speakers as wrong; 몰다 only fits motorized vehicles like 차/오토바이 or animals being driven (소떼를 몰다).

호 is the counter for issues of periodicals (magazines, journals, newsletters), not for 책 in the general 'book' sense. Calling a 책 'the 5호' implies it is issue #5 of a serial — odd for a generic book. Standard counter for books is 권. Also 제5호 is conventionally written without an internal space.
flagged.suggestion: 이 잡지는 제5호예요. (or, for a book: 이 책은 제5권이에요.)

flagged.issue: Word order is reversed. The natural Korean for 'powdered/icing sugar' is 가루 설탕 (modifier-head: powder-form sugar) or 슈가 파우더. 설탕 가루 (sugar's powder) reads as a redundant tautology since 설탕 itself already denotes a granular substance. Native bakers say 가루 설탕을 뿌려요.

Two issues. (1) 부 is the counter for printed copies of newspapers/documents/the same-edition reprint of a book; the unmarked counter for books is 권 (책 두 권). (2) The numeral-counter-의-noun structure (두 부의 책) is stilted; native pattern places the counter phrase post-nominally: 책 두 부를 빌렸어요. Combined, the sentence sounds translation-flavored.
flagged.suggestion: 책을 두 권 빌렸어요. (or, if the same-copy sense is intended: 그 책을 두 부 빌렸어요.)

flagged.issue: While 멋이 있다 is grammatically possible, native speakers overwhelmingly use the contracted adjective 멋있다 to mean 'is stylish/cool'. The decomposed form 멋이 있다 with a topic-marked location (옷에는) reads as a stilted calque ('there is style in his clothes'). Standard: 그의 옷이 멋있어요.

The standard term for the body of traffic rules drivers/pedestrians follow is 교통 법규 or 교통 규칙 (or the formal statute name 도로교통법, no internal space). 교통 법 (with a space, just '법') is unidiomatic — 법 alone is the abstract noun 'law' and pairs with major bodies of law (헌법, 형법) rather than with everyday compliance. Native speakers say 교통 법규를 지키다 / 교통 규칙을 지키다.

묻다 'to ask' is a ㄷ-irregular verb: ㄷ → ㄹ before a vowel, so the past tense is 물었어요, not 묻었어요. The form 묻었어요 is the regular conjugation of the homonym 묻다 'to bury' — semantically wrong here. Standard form: 선생님께 길을 물었어요.
